Take-home Exercise 2

Author

Jeounghyun Kim

Published

October 18, 2025

Modified

October 23, 2025

1. Overview

Efficient urban mobility is critical to Singapore’s economic vitality and quality of life.
As a dense city-state, Singapore relies heavily on its public bus network to connect residential heartlands with commercial hubs and essential services.

However, travel demand is far from uniform — it fluctuates sharply across space and time, creating complex mobility patterns.
Managing peak-hour congestion and adapting to shifting post-pandemic travel behaviors require a deep, data-driven understanding that goes beyond simple city-wide averages.

1.1 Objectives

The objective of this study is to analyze spatiotemporal patterns of bus passenger trips in Singapore using advanced spatial statistical techniques.

Specifically, the analysis aims to:

  1. Visualize the spatial distribution of passenger boardings by aggregating origin–destination (OD) data to a uniform 375 m hexagonal grid, ensuring spatial comparability.

  2. Assess global spatial autocorrelation of passenger volumes across different time slots using Global Moran’s I to determine whether spatial clustering exists at the overall study area level.

  3. Identify local spatial clusters and outliers by applying both Local Moran’s I and Local Geary’s C statistics at the hexagon level to detect hot spots and cold spots of passenger activity.

  4. Evaluate temporal dynamics of emerging and diminishing clusters using the Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), integrating the Getis–Ord Gi* statistic and the Mann–Kendall trend test.

  5. Draw policy-relevant insights about passenger demand patterns across different time periods (weekday AM/PM peaks and weekend) to support sustainable and efficient urban mobility planning.

2. The Data

This study integrates multiple datasets to enable spatial and temporal analysis of bus passenger patterns in Singapore.

2.1 Data Sources

Dataset Description Source
LTA Passenger Volume by Origin–Destination Bus Stops Monthly record of boarding and alighting passenger counts aggregated by bus stop pairs. Used to estimate passenger origins. LTA DataMall
Bus Stop Location Geospatial coordinates (WGS84) of each bus stop. Used to spatially link OD data. LTA DataMall
URA Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) KML polygon layer defining Singapore’s subzones. Used for contextual mapping. data.gov.sg
Hexagonal Grid (375 m) Custom tessellation created to enable consistent areal analysis. Derived using sf package

2.2 Spatial Unit and Temporal Scope

  • Spatial Unit: Each bus stop is spatially joined to a 375 m hexagonal cell. This minimizes the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) and provides balanced spatial granularity.

  • Temporal Scope: Passenger volumes are aggregated into three time slots:

    • Weekday AM Peak (06:00–09:00)

    • Weekday PM Peak (17:00–20:00)

    • Weekend / Public Holiday Midday (11:00–20:00)

2.3 Derived Variables

Variable Description
tap_on Total passenger boardings per hexagon per time slot.
density_norm (defined but not used in final models) Normalized passenger volume by area or number of stops.
region (defined but not used in final models) Regional label derived from URA Master Plan.

2.4 Data Cleaning and Integration

  1. Import KML file and extract REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, and SUBZONE_N fields using HTML parsing (rvest).

  2. Import bus stop and OD data from DataMall (read_csv).

  3. Use `st_join(…, join = st_within)` to assign each bus stop to its corresponding hexagonal cell; boundary gaps are handled later through validity checks and zero-preserving expansion.

  4. Aggregate boardings by hexagon × time slot.

  5. Save processed data as .rds for efficiency and reproducibility.

3. Setup and Preparation

3.1 Required R Packages

The analysis was conducted in R (version 4.4.1) using the following packages:

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse, rvest, spdep, sfdep, Kendall)

  • sf — handles geospatial vector data and performs spatial operations such as joins, intersections, and geometry validation.

  • tmap — creates both static and interactive thematic maps for spatial visualisation.

  • tidyverse — provides a cohesive toolkit for data import, wrangling, and transformation (notably readr, dplyr, and tidyr).

  • rvest — used to parse HTML metadata embedded within the URA Master Plan 2019 KML file.

  • spdep / sfdep — enable spatial autocorrelation and local cluster analysis, including LISA and Getis–Ord Gi* statistics, as well as the spatio-temporal framework required for Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA).

  • Kendall — performs the Mann–Kendall trend test, which detects increasing or decreasing trends in the spatio-temporal Gi* values during EHSA.

3.2 Directory and File Setup

All datasets are organized into two main folders within the project directory to ensure reproducibility and clarity of data sources.

Take-home_Ex02/
├── data/
│   ├── geospatial/   # BusStop shapefile (+dbf/shx/prj) and     MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml
│   ├── aspatial/     # LTA OD CSVs (202507–202509); EHSA uses 3-month series
│   └── rds/          # Processed R objects (e.g., hex_counts_sf.rds)
├── images/           # Exported maps and figures for the report
└── Take-home_Ex02.qmd # Main Quarto document (full workflow: data wrangling to EHSA)

  • data/geospatial/ — stores all spatial boundary and coordinate data, including: BusStop.shp and its associated files (.dbf, .shx, .prj, etc.) obtained from LTA DataMall, representing all active bus stop locations in Singapore.

  • MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml from Singapore’s URA Master Plan 2019, used as the administrative boundary layer for spatial joins and clipping.

  • data/aspatial/ — contains LTA Origin–Destination (OD) CSV files.

    Most analyses (e.g., LISA, Gi*) use September 2025 data only.

    The Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) combines three consecutive months (July–September 2025) to capture temporal trends.

  • data/rds/ — stores processed R objects such as hex_counts_sf.rds and hex_counts_sf_z.rds created during data aggregation and spatial analysis.

  • images/ — contains exported figures and maps generated via tmap_save() for use in the final report.

  • Take-home_Ex02.qmd — the main Quarto document encompassing the full workflow from data wrangling to EHSA, ensuring reproducibility.

3.3 Data Wrangling

Goal: Read geospatial/aspatial data, parse KML metadata, harmonize CRS, create a 375 m hexagonal grid, map bus stops to hexagons, and aggregate origin trips by required time slots while preserving zero-count cells.

3.3.1 Import geospatial data (URA KML & Bus Stops)

The URA Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary KML file was first imported and cleaned.
As KML files store attribute information in HTML format under the Description field, the relevant metadata (REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, SUBZONE_N, and SUBZONE_C) was parsed using the rvest package.
All geometries were projected to SVY21 (EPSG:3414) for spatial alignment with other datasets.

Next, the LTA Bus Stop shapefile was loaded and reprojected to the same CRS.
Only bus stops within Singapore’s land boundary were retained using a spatial intersection with the Master Plan polygon.
This ensured that subsequent trip mapping was geographically consistent and excluded offshore or null points.

# URA MP2019 Subzone Boundary (KML)
mp19_raw <- sf::st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml")

# Parse KML Description HTML to extract fields
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
page <- rvest::read_html(html_text)
rows <- page %>% rvest::html_elements("tr")
value <- rows %>%
purrr::keep(~ rvest::html_text2(rvest::html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
rvest::html_element("td") %>%
rvest::html_text2()
if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mp19 <- mp19 %>%
dplyr::mutate(
REGION_N = purrr::map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
PLN_AREA_N = purrr::map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
SUBZONE_N = purrr::map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
SUBZONE_C = purrr::map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
) %>%
dplyr::select(REGION_N, PLN_AREA_N, SUBZONE_N, SUBZONE_C, geometry)

# Bus Stop shapefile (keep all associated files together in geospatial/)
bus_stop_sf <- sf::st_read("data/geospatial/BusStop.shp")

# Unify CRS to SVY21 for analysis
mp19_3414 <- st_transform(mp19, 3414)
bus_stop_3414 <- st_transform(bus_stop_sf, 3414)

3.3.2 Create a 375 m hexagon grid

The task requires creating a hexagonal grid where each cell has an apothegm of 375 m. The apothegm is the perpendicular distance from the center of the hexagon to any of its sides.

The sf::st_make_grid() function creates flat-topped hexagons when square = FALSE. For this function, the cellsizeargument defines the “flat-to-flat” distance (F) — the total height of the hexagon, or the distance between two opposite parallel sides.

The geometric relationship between the apothegm (a) and the flat-to-flat distance (F) is: F=2×a

Therefore, to create a hexagon grid with an apothegm of 375 m, we must set the cellsize parameter to: cellsize = 2 × 375 m = 750 m

# Disable spherical geometry engine to ensure planar calculations (SVY21 projection)
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

# --- Step 1: Define hexagon grid parameters ---
a <- 375                      # apothem distance (center to edge)
cell_size <- 2 * a            # flat-to-flat distance = 750 m

# --- Step 2: Generate hexagonal grid covering Singapore land area ---
hexagon <- st_make_grid(
  mp19_3414,                  # Master Plan 2019 Subzone boundary (in EPSG:3414)
  cellsize = cell_size,       # grid size (750 m)
  square   = FALSE,           # create hexagons instead of squares
  what     = "polygons"       # output polygon geometries
) |>
  st_sf() |>
  st_intersection(st_union(mp19_3414)) |>  # clip to Singapore mainland boundary
  st_make_valid()                          # ensure valid geometries

# Assign unique hexagon IDs
hexagon$hex_id <- sprintf("H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon)))

# --- Step 3: Remove isolated/offshore hexagons (retain only those containing bus stops) ---
BusStop_in_SG <- sf::st_join(
  bus_stop_3414 %>% dplyr::select(geometry),  # bus stop points (EPSG:3414)
  mp19_3414,                                 # Singapore mainland boundary
  join = sf::st_within,                      # keep points within mainland polygons
  left  = FALSE
)

# Count number of bus stops intersecting each hexagon
hexagon$n_collisions <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(hexagon, BusStop_in_SG))

# Keep only hexagons that contain at least one bus stop
hexagon <- dplyr::filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0) %>%
  dplyr::select(-n_collisions)
summary(as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(hexagon), "km^2")))
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
0.03517 0.48714 0.48714 0.47596 0.48714 0.48714

This calculation ensures each hexagon has the correct area of approximately 0.487 km² (Area=23​×a2), providing a suitable Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ) size that balances neighborhood-level resolution and computational efficiency.

3.3.3 Import OD table and prepare time slots

The aspatial OD dataset (origin_destination_bus_202509.csv) was imported next.
Because DataMall schema versions vary across months, column names were dynamically detected to standardize key variables:

  • ORIGIN, DEST, HOUR, DAYT, and TRIPS

A helper function was applied to classify each trip record into one of three time slots based on DAY_TYPE and HOUR:

  • WKDY_AM_06_09: Weekday morning peak

  • WKDY_PM_17_20: Weekday evening peak

  • WKND_11_20: Weekend/holiday period

Invalid or missing records were removed to ensure clean aggregation.

# 1) Read CSV (quiet)
od_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  "data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202509.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# 2) Detect actual column names present in this file
nm <- names(od_raw)
pick_first <- function(cands) {
  hit <- intersect(cands, nm)
  if (length(hit) == 0) NA_character_ else hit[1]
}

origin_col <- pick_first(c("ORIGIN_PT_CODE","ORIGIN_BS","origin"))
dest_col   <- pick_first(c("DESTINATION_PT_CODE","DEST_BS","destination"))
hour_col   <- pick_first(c("TIME_PER_HOUR","HOUR","PT_TIME"))
dayt_col   <- pick_first(c("DAY_TYPE","DAYTYPE"))
trips_col  <- pick_first(c("TOTAL_TRIPS","TRIPS"))

# (optional) fail fast if any required field is missing
stopifnot(!is.na(origin_col), !is.na(dest_col),
          !is.na(hour_col),   !is.na(dayt_col),
          !is.na(trips_col))

# 3) Standardize column names
od <- od_raw %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    ORIGIN = dplyr::all_of(origin_col),
    DEST   = dplyr::all_of(dest_col),
    HOUR   = dplyr::all_of(hour_col),
    DAYT   = dplyr::all_of(dayt_col),
    TRIPS  = dplyr::all_of(trips_col)
  )

# 4) Slot classifier (weekday/weekend-holiday)
slot_from_day_hour <- function(day_type, hour) {
  dt <- toupper(trimws(as.character(day_type)))
  if (is.na(hour)) return(NA_character_)
  weekend_tokens <- c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY","WEEKEND","HOLIDAY","WEEKEND/PH","WEEKEND/PHOLIDAY")
  if (dt %in% weekend_tokens) {
    if (hour >= 11 & hour < 20) "WKND_11_20" else NA_character_
  } else {
    if (hour >=  6 & hour <  9) "WKDY_AM_06_09" else
    if (hour >= 17 & hour < 20) "WKDY_PM_17_20" else NA_character_
  }
}

# 5) Clean types + derive slot + filter valid rows
od <- od %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    ORIGIN = as.character(ORIGIN),
    DEST   = as.character(DEST),
    HOUR   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(HOUR)),
    TRIPS  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(TRIPS)),
    slot   = purrr::pmap_chr(list(DAYT, HOUR), slot_from_day_hour)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(slot), !is.na(ORIGIN), !is.na(TRIPS))

3.3.4 Map Bus Stops to Hexagons and Aggregate Trips

Each bus stop was spatially joined to its corresponding hexagon using st_intersects(), ensuring that even stops located along hexagon boundaries were properly included.
This spatial join allowed all origin points to inherit a hex_id.
Trip counts were then aggregated by hex_id and slot using dplyr, while preserving zero-count hexagons to maintain full spatial coverage.
The resulting dataset provides a hexagon-level summary of total passenger boardings per time slot, forming the foundation for subsequent Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA), Global and Local Spatial Autocorrelation, and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis in later sections.

stopifnot(exists("hexagon"), exists("od"))

# Disable spherical geometry engine to ensure planar calculations under EPSG:3414
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
hexagon <- hexagon %>% st_make_valid()

# --- Step 1: Standardize bus stop codes across different naming conventions ---
pick_first <- function(cands, pool) {
  hit <- intersect(cands, pool)
  if (length(hit) == 0) NA_character_ else hit[1]
}

# Identify the correct bus stop code column
bs_code_col <- pick_first(
  c("BUS_STOP_CODE","BusStopCode","BUS_STOP_N","BUSSTOP_N","BUS_STOP_NO",
    "BUSSTOPCODE","STOP_CODE","CODE","BUS_CODE","BUSSTOP","STOPID","STOP_ID"),
  names(bus_stop_3414)
)
stopifnot(!is.na(bs_code_col))

# Rename and pad all bus stop codes to consistent 5-digit format
bus_stop_3414 <- bus_stop_3414 %>%
  dplyr::rename(BUS_STOP_CODE = dplyr::all_of(bs_code_col)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(BUS_STOP_CODE = stringr::str_pad(as.character(BUS_STOP_CODE), width = 5, pad = "0"))

# --- Step 2: Spatially join bus stops to hexagons (assign each stop to one hex_id) ---
stop_hex <- sf::st_join(
  bus_stop_3414["BUS_STOP_CODE"],
  hexagon["hex_id"],
  join = sf::st_within,   # assign if the stop lies within a hexagon
  left = TRUE
) %>% 
  sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::distinct(BUS_STOP_CODE, hex_id)

# Print mapping success rate
message(sprintf("Mapped %d / %d stops (%.1f%%).",
                sum(!is.na(stop_hex$hex_id)), nrow(stop_hex),
                100 * mean(!is.na(stop_hex$hex_id))))

# --- Step 3: Assign each trip record to a hexagon based on ORIGIN bus stop ---
all_slots <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09","WKDY_PM_17_20","WKND_11_20")

od_hex <- od %>%
  dplyr::mutate(ORIGIN = stringr::str_pad(as.character(ORIGIN), width = 5, pad = "0")) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(stop_hex, by = c("ORIGIN" = "BUS_STOP_CODE")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(hex_id))   # remove trips with unmapped stops

# --- Step 4: Aggregate total trips per hexagon and time slot ---
hex_counts <- od_hex %>%
  dplyr::group_by(hex_id, slot) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(tap_on = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

# --- Step 5: Ensure zero-preserving structure (include all hex×slot combinations) ---
hex_slot_full <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  hex_id = hexagon$hex_id,
  slot   = all_slots
) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(hex_counts, by = c("hex_id","slot")) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    slot   = factor(slot, levels = all_slots),
    tap_on = dplyr::coalesce(tap_on, 0)   # replace missing with zero
  )

# --- Step 6: Merge with geometry for spatial analysis ---
hex_counts_sf <- hexagon %>%
  dplyr::left_join(hex_slot_full, by = "hex_id")

# --- Step 7: Save processed spatial dataset for later use ---
dir.create("data/rds", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
readr::write_rds(hex_counts_sf, "data/rds/hex_counts_sf.rds")

# --- Step 8: Quick validation checks ---
mean(!is.na(stop_hex$hex_id))   # proportion of mapped bus stops
[1] 0.9990303
mean(!is.na(od_hex$hex_id))     # proportion of mapped trip origins
[1] 1
summary(hex_counts$tap_on)      # summary of trip counts per hexagon
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
      1    2055   10780   22779   29452  421361 
sum(hex_counts$tap_on > 0)      # number of non-zero hexagons
[1] 2455
# Validation of Wrangling Results
# 1. Bus Stop → Hexagon mapping success rate
mean(!is.na(stop_hex$hex_id))
[1] 0.9990303
# 2. OD records with valid hex_id
mean(!is.na(od_hex$hex_id))
[1] 1
# 3. Summary of aggregated trips
summary(hex_counts$tap_on)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
      1    2055   10780   22779   29452  421361 
# 4. Number of non-zero hexagons
sum(hex_counts$tap_on > 0)

A quick validation confirmed that 99.9% of bus stops were successfully matched to hexagons, and all OD records received valid hex_id assignments.
The aggregated trip counts ranged from 1 to 421,361, indicating a highly skewed distribution where most hexagons have relatively low boarding volumes, while a few central zones exhibit very high concentrations.
Out of all hexagons, 2,455 recorded at least one boarding, confirming that zero-preserving aggregation worked as intended. Together, these checks confirm that the dataset is spatially complete, internally consistent, and ready for subsequent spatial analysis.

4. Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA)

4.1 Visual Exploration of Passenger Boardings

After completing the data wrangling, I first visualized how passenger boardings are distributed across Singapore.
This step focuses on understanding spatial patterns before moving into formal spatial statistics.

By mapping aggregated tap_on values across different time slots, it becomes easier to see which areas consistently show higher boarding activity and how those patterns differ between weekday peaks and weekends.

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(hex_counts_sf) +
  tm_polygons("tap_on",
              breaks = c(-Inf, 0, Inf), palette = c("grey90", NA),
              title = "Total Tap-on (0 shown in grey)") +
tm_shape(subset(hex_counts_sf, tap_on > 0)) +
  tm_polygons("tap_on",
              style = "quantile", n = 5, palette = "Blues",
              title = "Total Tap-on (>0)") +
  tm_facets(by = "slot", ncol = 3) +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Passenger Boardings by Time Slot",
            legend.outside = TRUE)

The visualization shows clear spatial differences in boarding activity across Singapore.
Darker blue areas indicate higher passenger volumes, especially around major transport hubs such as the CBD, Tampines, Woodlands, and Jurong East, reflecting key commuting corridors.
Lighter blue or grey zones represent areas with low or no boardings, often corresponding to residential or peripheral regions.
Overall, the map confirms that the spatial aggregation worked as intended and sets up the next part of the analysis.

4.2 Global Spatial Autocorrelation (Moran’s I)

This section examines whether passenger boardings (tap_on) are spatially clustered across Singapore.
Using Global Moran’s I, we can determine if high-boarding areas tend to be near other high-boarding areas (positive spatial autocorrelation),
or if the pattern appears more random or dispersed.

A significantly positive Moran’s I value indicates that similar values (e.g., high boardings) are spatially clustered,
while a value close to zero suggests randomness, and a negative value implies a dispersed pattern.

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

# 1) Create a base geometry using one time slot (fixed row order)
#    → ensures consistent neighbor structure across all time slots
hex_base_geom <- hex_counts_sf %>%
  dplyr::filter(slot == "WKDY_AM_06_09") %>%
  dplyr::select(hex_id) %>%
  sf::st_as_sf()

# 2) Build neighborhood and spatial weights (Queen contiguity)
#    Use a small snap tolerance to fix minor boundary gaps
nb_hex <- spdep::poly2nb(hex_base_geom, queen = TRUE, snap = 2)
lw_hex <- spdep::nb2listw(nb_hex, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# 3) Extract values by slot in the same geometric order → compute Moran’s I
all_slots <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09", "WKDY_PM_17_20", "WKND_11_20")

global_moran_results <- purrr::map_dfr(all_slots, ~{
  slot_data <- hex_base_geom %>%
    dplyr::left_join(
      hex_counts_sf %>%
        sf::st_drop_geometry() %>%
        dplyr::filter(slot == .x) %>%
        dplyr::select(hex_id, tap_on),
      by = "hex_id"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(tap_on = dplyr::coalesce(tap_on, 0))

  # Run Global Moran’s I test using the same spatial weights
  test_result <- spdep::moran.test(slot_data$tap_on, lw_hex, zero.policy = TRUE)

  # Store results in a clean summary table
  tibble::tibble(
    `Time Slot` = .x,
    `Moran I Statistic` = unname(test_result$estimate["Moran I statistic"]),
    `p-value` = test_result$p.value
  )
})

# 4) Display results as a formatted table
knitr::kable(global_moran_results, digits = c(NA, 4, 16),
             caption = "Global Moran's I Results by Time Slot")
Global Moran’s I Results by Time Slot
Time Slot Moran I Statistic p-value
WKDY_AM_06_09 0.3532 0.000000e+00
WKDY_PM_17_20 0.1343 1.844094e-09
WKND_11_20 0.2273 0.000000e+00

To assess the overall spatial clustering across the entire study area, Global Moran’s I was calculated for each time slot.

Statistical Significance: All three time slots show extremely small p-values (≈ 0 or < 2.2e−16), indicating that the observed bus boarding patterns are not random and possess a statistically significant spatial structure.

Presence of Clustering: All three Moran’s I statistics are positive (0.3532, 0.1343, 0.2273), confirming the presence of positive spatial autocorrelation. In other words, hexagons with high boarding volumes tend to be located near other high-volume hexagons, while low-volume areas are surrounded by similarly low-volume neighbors. This clustering tendency is consistently observed across all three time periods.

Variation in Clustering Strength: The magnitude of Moran’s I differs across time slots, revealing temporal variation in clustering intensity.

– Weekday AM Peak (I = 0.3532): The strongest spatial clustering, indicating concentrated morning boardings around major employment and transfer hubs.

– Weekday PM Peak (I = 0.1343): The weakest clustering, reflecting a more dispersed pattern of evening return trips.

– Weekend (I = 0.2273): A moderate clustering strength, likely driven by leisure and shopping activities.

Note

(Minor “no neighbours” warnings are expected due to offshore islands and are handled using zero.policy = TRUE.)

4.3 Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA)

While the Global Moran’s I test confirmed the overall presence of spatial clustering, it does not reveal where these clusters occur. To gain deeper insight into the spatial distribution of passenger boardings, Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) were applied.

These methods — including Local Moran’s I (LISA), Local Geary’s C, and Getis–Ord Gi* — capture spatial dependence at the neighborhood level. Together, they help identify where clustering occurs, how similar or different adjacent areas are, and how strong these local concentrations are.

4.3.1 Local Moran’s I (LISA)

Local Moran’s I (LISA) identifies individual hexagons that form statistically significant local clusters — either High–High (hot spots), where high boarding volumes are surrounded by similarly high values, or Low–Low (cold spots), where low-volume areas cluster together. Transitional patterns such as High–Low or Low–High indicate spatial outliers.

plot_lisa_one_slot <- function(sf_all, slot_label, var = "tap_on", alpha = 0.05) {
  tmap_mode("plot")
  sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

  # 1) Select one time slot, validate geometries, and remove missing values
  df <- sf_all %>%
    filter(slot == slot_label) %>%
    st_make_valid() %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))

  # Safety check: if all values are missing or have no variance, skip analysis
  x_raw <- df[[var]]
  if (all(is.na(x_raw)) || length(unique(x_raw)) <= 1) {
    message(sprintf("[LISA] '%s' slot: no variance → LISA skipped", slot_label))
    return(
      tm_shape(df) + tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.alpha = 0) +
        tm_layout(main.title = paste("LISA —", slot_label, "(no variance)"))
    )
  }

  # 2) Build neighborhood structure and spatial weights (Queen contiguity)
  # Use small snap tolerance to handle boundary gaps, allow zero neighbors
  nb <- poly2nb(df, queen = TRUE, snap = 2)

  # Identify polygons with no neighbors
  no_neigh <- card(nb) == 0
  if (any(no_neigh)) {
    # Remove those polygons to maintain consistency between df and nb
    keep_idx <- which(!no_neigh)
    df <- df[keep_idx, ]
    nb <- subset(nb, !no_neigh)
  }

  # Create row-standardized spatial weights list
  lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

  # 3) Standardize variable and compute spatial lag
  x <- scale(df[[var]])[, 1]
  lag_x <- lag.listw(lw, x, zero.policy = TRUE)

  # 4) Compute Local Moran’s I statistic using spdep
  lm_out <- localmoran(x, lw, zero.policy = TRUE) %>% as.data.frame()

  # spdep output columns: Ii, E.Ii, Var.Ii, Z.Ii, Pr(z > 0)
  colnames(lm_out) <- c("Ii","E_Ii","Var_Ii","Z_Ii","p_value")

  # Combine results with original spatial data
  df <- bind_cols(df, lm_out)

  # 5) Classify quadrants (spatial association type) and filter significant ones
  df <- df %>%
    mutate(
      quad = case_when(
        x > 0 & lag_x > 0 ~ "High-High",
        x < 0 & lag_x < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
        x > 0 & lag_x < 0 ~ "High-Low",
        x < 0 & lag_x > 0 ~ "Low-High",
        TRUE ~ "Not Sig"
      ),
      quad = ifelse(p_value < alpha, quad, "Not Sig")
    )

  # Keep only statistically significant observations
  df_sig <- df %>% filter(quad != "Not Sig")

  # 6) Visualization using tmap
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(col = "grey95", border.alpha = 0) +   # background polygons
  tm_shape(df_sig) +
    tm_polygons("quad",
      palette = c("High-High"="#d73027","Low-Low"="#4575b4",
                  "High-Low"="#fdae61","Low-High"="#74add1"),
      title = paste0("Local Moran’s I (p<", alpha, ")")
    ) +
    tm_layout(main.title = paste("LISA —", slot_label),
              legend.outside = TRUE)
}

# Define the three time slots and generate LISA maps for each
slots <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09","WKDY_PM_17_20","WKND_11_20")
for (s in slots) print(plot_lisa_one_slot(hex_counts_sf, s))

Weekday AM Peak (06–09):
The LISA map for the morning peak reveals extensive High–High clusters (red) concentrated around Singapore’s key employment and interchange areas, such as the Central Business District, Tampines, Woodlands, and Jurong East. These locations indicate high boarding volumes surrounded by other high values, reflecting strong spatial clustering of commuter demand during morning hours. A few Low–High outliers (blue) are observed near residential zones adjacent to these hubs, where local boarding intensity is relatively low despite being near high-demand areas.

Weekday PM Peak (17–20):
Compared to the morning, the evening peak shows fewer and more scattered clusters, suggesting a more spatially dispersed pattern of return trips. High–High clusters remain visible near major residential towns and interchanges but appear weaker and more fragmented, indicating that evening trips are distributed across multiple destinations.

Weekend (11–20):
During the weekend, High–High clusters reappear around both central and suburban leisure or shopping districts (e.g., Orchard, Tampines, Jurong), indicating strong boarding activity linked to recreational travel. The clustering pattern is broader than the weekday evening but less concentrated than the weekday morning, reflecting moderate spatial clustering of leisure-related mobility.

4.3.2 Local Geary’s C

Building upon the LISA findings, Local Geary’s C further examines how similar or dissimilar each hexagon is compared to its neighbours, revealing subtle transitions within and between clusters.

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
tmap_mode("plot")

plot_geary_one_slot <- function(sf_all, slot_label, var = "tap_on", alpha = 0.05) {
  # 1) Select target slot and validate geometry
  df <- sf_all %>%
    filter(slot == slot_label) %>%
    st_make_valid() %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))

  # Skip if not enough variation
  if (nrow(df) == 0 || length(unique(df[[var]])) <= 1) {
    message(sprintf("[GearyC] '%s' slot: insufficient variation, skipped.", slot_label))
    return(NULL)
  }

  # 2) Build neighborhood structure (Queen contiguity + snap)
  nb <- poly2nb(df, queen = TRUE, snap = 2)
  no_neigh <- card(nb) == 0
  if (any(no_neigh)) {
    keep_idx <- which(!no_neigh)
    df <- df[keep_idx, ]
    nb <- subset(nb, !no_neigh)
  }
  lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

  # 3) Compute Local Geary’s C
  lc <- localC(df[[var]], lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
  df$localC <- lc

  # 4) Standardize results (Z-score approximation)
  z_lc <- scale(lc)
  df$z_score <- as.numeric(z_lc)
  df$sig <- ifelse(abs(z_lc) > qnorm(1 - alpha/2), "Significant", "Not Sig")

  # 5) Visualization
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons("z_score",
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                palette = "RdBu",
                title = "Local Geary’s C (Z-score)") +
    tm_borders(col = "gray60") +
    tm_layout(main.title = paste("Local Geary’s C —", slot_label),
              legend.outside = TRUE)
}

# Run for all three time slots
slots <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09", "WKDY_PM_17_20", "WKND_11_20")
for (s in slots) print(plot_geary_one_slot(hex_counts_sf, s))

Although the spatial patterns revealed by Local Geary’s C are broadly consistent with those identified by the Local Moran’s I (LISA) analysis, the Geary’s C maps display slightly wider red regions indicating strong local similarity. This difference arises from the conceptual focus of the two statistics.

LISA emphasizes the direction of spatial association, identifying where high or low values cluster together (e.g., High–High or Low–Low regions). In contrast, Local Geary’s C measures the degree of local dissimilarity, capturing how similar or different each area is compared to its neighbors. As a result, areas with very similar values—regardless of whether they are high or low—exhibit low Geary’s C values and are shown in red.

Consequently, Geary’s C not only reaffirms the key clusters detected by LISA (e.g., CBD, Tampines, Jurong East) but also highlights transitional zones and boundary regions where spatial similarity gradually changes. Together, the two measures provide a more comprehensive understanding of both cluster strength and internal homogeneity within Singapore’s urban mobility patterns.

4.3.3 Getis–Ord Gi* Statistic

Complementing both Local Moran’s I and Local Geary’s C analyses, the Getis–Ord Gi* statistic focuses on identifying where clusters of high or low passenger activity are most intense.

While the previous measures emphasized spatial association and similarity between neighboring hexagons, Gi* highlights the strength and persistence of clustering, revealing statistically significant hot and cold spots across different time periods.

This helps reveal whether certain regions consistently experience high passenger activity (hot spots) or low activity (cold spots) during each time period.

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
tmap::tmap_mode("plot")

plot_gistar_one_slot <- function(sf_all, slot_label, var = "tap_on", alpha = 0.05) {
  
  # 1) Filter one time slot
  df <- sf_all %>%
    dplyr::filter(slot == slot_label) %>%
    sf::st_make_valid() %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data[[var]]))
  
  if (nrow(df) == 0 || length(unique(df[[var]])) <= 1) {
    message(sprintf("[Gi*] '%s': insufficient variation → skipped", slot_label))
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # 2) Build neighborhood and weights
  nb <- spdep::poly2nb(df, queen = TRUE, snap = 2)
  no_neigh <- spdep::card(nb) == 0
  if (any(no_neigh)) {
    keep_idx <- which(!no_neigh)
    df <- df[keep_idx, ]
    nb <- subset(nb, !no_neigh)
  }
  wt <- spdep::nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  
  # 3) Compute Getis–Ord Gi*
  gi <- sfdep::local_gstar_perm(
    x = df[[var]],
    nb = nb,
    wt = wt,
    nsim = 199,
    alternative = "two.sided"
  )
  
  gi_df <- as.data.frame(gi)
  if (!"p_value" %in% names(gi_df) && "z_score" %in% names(gi_df)) {
    gi_df$p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(gi_df$z_score))
  }
  
  df$z_score <- gi_df$z_score
  df$p_value <- gi_df$p_value
  
  df_sig <- df %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(p_value) & p_value < alpha)
  
  # 4) Plot (tmap v4 syntax)
  if (nrow(df_sig) == 0) {
    return(
      tmap::tm_shape(df) +
        tmap::tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "white") +
        tmap::tm_title(paste0("Getis–Ord Gi* — ", slot_label, " (no p<", alpha, " cells)")) +
        tmap::tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
    )
  }
  
  tmap::tm_shape(df) +
    tmap::tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "white") +
  tmap::tm_shape(df_sig) +
    tmap::tm_polygons(
      fill = df_sig$z_score,
      fill.scale = tmap::tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 5, values = "-RdBu"),
      fill.legend = tmap::tm_legend(title = "Gi* z-score")
    ) +
    tmap::tm_title(paste0("Getis–Ord Gi* — ", slot_label, " (p<", alpha, ")")) +
    tmap::tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}

# ── Run for each time slot ─────────────────────────────
stopifnot(exists("hex_counts_sf"))
slots <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09", "WKDY_PM_17_20", "WKND_11_20")

for (s in slots) {
  print(plot_gistar_one_slot(hex_counts_sf, s))
}

The Getis–Ord Gi* statistic highlights clusters where high passenger activity is concentrated across different regions.

During weekday mornings (06–09), hot spots appear mainly in northern (Woodlands, Yishun) and eastern (Tampines, Pasir Ris) areas, reflecting strong outbound commuting from residential zones toward central business districts.
In the weekday evening period (17–20), the clusters shift toward downtown and western employment hubs (Jurong East, Boon Lay), showing return trips during the homebound hours.
By contrast, the weekend (11–20) pattern becomes more spatially balanced, with clusters around Orchard, Tampines, and Jurong, indicating leisure-oriented movements rather than work-based travel. Overall, the Gi* results reinforce the LISA findings but place greater emphasis on the intensity and persistence of high-demand clusters, showing how passenger activity levels vary across time slots.

4.4 Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)

In this study, EHSA was applied to analyse how passenger boarding hot spots have evolved across three time intervals — weekday morning, weekday evening, and weekend.
By integrating the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic and the Mann-Kendall trend test, this method reveals whether passenger demand in each hexagon is intensifying, diminishing, or remaining stable over time.

# Function: Read and standardize monthly OD data 
read_od_month <- function(path, ym_label) {
  x <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  nm <- names(x)
  
  # Helper function: pick the first matching column name
  pick_first <- function(cands) { 
    h <- intersect(cands, nm)
    if (length(h) == 0) NA_character_ else h[1] 
  }
  
  # Automatically detect column names for origin, hour, day type, and trips
  origin_col <- pick_first(c("ORIGIN_PT_CODE","ORIGIN_BS","origin"))
  hour_col   <- pick_first(c("TIME_PER_HOUR","HOUR","PT_TIME"))
  dayt_col   <- pick_first(c("DAY_TYPE","DAYTYPE"))
  trips_col  <- pick_first(c("TOTAL_TRIPS","TRIPS"))
  stopifnot(!is.na(origin_col), !is.na(hour_col), !is.na(dayt_col), !is.na(trips_col))

  # Classify each record into time slots based on day type and hour
  slot_from_day_hour <- function(day_type, hour) {
    dt <- toupper(trimws(as.character(day_type)))
    if (is.na(hour)) return(NA_character_)
    
    # Define weekend tokens
    weekend_tokens <- c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY","WEEKEND","HOLIDAY","WEEKEND/PH","WEEKEND/PHOLIDAY")
    
    # Assign slot category
    if (dt %in% weekend_tokens) {
      if (hour >= 11 & hour < 20) "WKND_11_20" else NA_character_
    } else {
      if (hour >= 6 & hour < 9) "WKDY_AM_06_09" else
      if (hour >= 17 & hour < 20) "WKDY_PM_17_20" else NA_character_
    }
  }

  # Extract and standardize relevant columns
  x %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      ORIGIN = as.character(.data[[origin_col]]),
      HOUR   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(.data[[hour_col]])),
      DAYT   = .data[[dayt_col]],
      TRIPS  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.data[[trips_col]])),
      slot   = purrr::pmap_chr(list(DAYT, HOUR), slot_from_day_hour),
      month  = ym_label
    ) %>%
    # Keep only valid records
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(slot), !is.na(ORIGIN), !is.na(TRIPS))
}

# ── Use the previously defined monthly OD reading and standardization function ──
read_od_month <- function(path, ym_label) {
  x <- readr::read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE)
  nm <- names(x)
  
  # Helper: automatically detect column names
  pick_first <- function(cands) { 
    h <- intersect(cands, nm)
    if (length(h) == 0) NA_character_ else h[1] 
  }
  origin_col <- pick_first(c("ORIGIN_PT_CODE","ORIGIN_BS","origin"))
  hour_col   <- pick_first(c("TIME_PER_HOUR","HOUR","PT_TIME"))
  dayt_col   <- pick_first(c("DAY_TYPE","DAYTYPE"))
  trips_col  <- pick_first(c("TOTAL_TRIPS","TRIPS"))
  stopifnot(!is.na(origin_col), !is.na(hour_col), !is.na(dayt_col), !is.na(trips_col))

  # Function to assign time slot based on day type and hour
  slot_from_day_hour <- function(day_type, hour) {
    dt <- toupper(trimws(as.character(day_type)))
    if (is.na(hour)) return(NA_character_)
    weekend_tokens <- c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY","WEEKEND","HOLIDAY","WEEKEND/PH","WEEKEND/PHOLIDAY")
    if (dt %in% weekend_tokens) {
      if (hour >= 11 & hour < 20) "WKND_11_20" else NA_character_
    } else {
      if (hour >= 6 & hour < 9) "WKDY_AM_06_09" else
      if (hour >= 17 & hour < 20) "WKDY_PM_17_20" else NA_character_
    }
  }

  x %>%
    dplyr::transmute(
      ORIGIN = as.character(.data[[origin_col]]),
      HOUR   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(.data[[hour_col]])),
      DAYT   = .data[[dayt_col]],
      TRIPS  = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.data[[trips_col]])),
      slot   = purrr::pmap_chr(list(DAYT, HOUR), slot_from_day_hour),
      month  = ym_label
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(slot), !is.na(ORIGIN), !is.na(TRIPS))
}

# Read monthly OD files (adjust the file paths as needed)
od_07 <- read_od_month("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202507.csv", "2025-07")
od_08 <- read_od_month("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv", "2025-08")
od_09 <- read_od_month("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202509.csv", "2025-09")
od_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(od_07, od_08, od_09)

# 1) Helper: Left-pad bus stop codes to 5 digits --------------------------------
pad5 <- function(x) stringr::str_pad(as.character(x), width = 5, side = "left", pad = "0")

# 2) Verify bus stop code column and create mapping table (stop2hex) ------------
bs_code_col <- intersect(c("BUS_STOP_CODE","BUS_STOP_N","BusStopCode"), names(bus_stop_3414))[1]
stopifnot(!is.na(bs_code_col))

# Preserve geometry by selecting only hex_id (geometry is automatically retained)
stop2hex_raw <- bus_stop_3414 %>%
  rename(BUS_STOP_CODE = all_of(bs_code_col)) %>%
  mutate(BUS_STOP_CODE = pad5(BUS_STOP_CODE)) %>%
  st_join(select(hexagon, hex_id), join = st_within) %>%
  filter(!is.na(hex_id))

# Avoid many-to-many relationships by keeping only the nearest hexagon (↑ reproducibility)
# (Use direct distance between bus stop points and hexagon centroids)
stop2hex <- stop2hex_raw %>%
  group_by(BUS_STOP_CODE) %>%
  slice_min(
    order_by = st_distance(
      geometry, 
      st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(select(hexagon, hex_id))[match(hex_id, hexagon$hex_id)])
    ),
    n = 1, with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  distinct(BUS_STOP_CODE, hex_id)

# 3) Aggregate by month and slot  ←←★ (previously: month only; now: month + slot) -----
od_all <- od_all %>% mutate(ORIGIN = pad5(ORIGIN))
od_hex_m <- od_all %>%
  left_join(stop2hex, by = c("ORIGIN" = "BUS_STOP_CODE")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(hex_id)) %>%
  group_by(hex_id, month, slot) %>%
  summarise(tap_on = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

months_lv <- sort(unique(od_all$month))
slots_lv  <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09","WKDY_PM_17_20","WKND_11_20")

# 4) Build spatio-temporal panel (fill missing 0s + attach geometry)  ←←★ (slot added) -----
panel_m <- expand_grid(
  hex_id = hexagon$hex_id,
  month  = months_lv,
  slot   = slots_lv
) %>%
  left_join(od_hex_m, by = c("hex_id","month","slot")) %>%
  mutate(tap_on = coalesce(tap_on, 0)) %>%
  left_join(select(hexagon, hex_id), by = "hex_id") %>%  # geometry automatically included
  st_as_sf()

# 5) Remove invalid cells (zero variance or no activity across all periods) -------
keep_hex <- panel_m %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(hex_id, slot) %>%  # remove hexagons with no temporal variation per slot
  summarise(v = var(tap_on), nz = sum(tap_on > 0), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(!is.na(v), v > 0, nz > 0) %>%
  pull(hex_id) %>% unique()

panel_m <- panel_m %>% filter(hex_id %in% keep_hex)
# B) EHSA — Robust pipeline per time slot (+ batch runner)
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

# Sanity checks: required objects and columns
stopifnot(exists("panel_m"), exists("hexagon"))
stopifnot(inherits(hexagon, "sf"), "hex_id" %in% names(hexagon))
tmap_mode("plot")

# Function: run EHSA for a single time slot and return an sf with classifications
run_ehsa_for_slot <- function(target_slot,
                              nsim = 199,
                              k_lag = 1,
                              jitter_sd = 1e-6) {
  # 1) Filter the panel by slot and create a numeric time index (YYYYMM)
  pm <- panel_m %>% filter(slot == target_slot)
  stopifnot(nrow(pm) > 0)
  if (!"month_num" %in% names(pm)) {
    pm <- pm %>% mutate(month_num = as.numeric(gsub("-", "", month)))
  }
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(pm$month_num)))

  # 2) Build valid polygon layer for the set of hexagons present in this slot
  ids <- intersect(unique(pm$hex_id), unique(hexagon$hex_id))
  loc_geom <- hexagon %>%
    filter(hex_id %in% ids) %>%
    st_make_valid() %>%
    st_collection_extract("POLYGON", warn = FALSE)
  loc_geom <- loc_geom[!st_is_empty(loc_geom), , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(loc_geom) < 2) stop("Fewer than 2 valid polygons. Check hexagon layer or filters.")

  # 3) Complete panel (hex_id × month) → fill missing with 0, standardize, and add tiny jitter
  months_lv <- sort(unique(pm$month_num))
  keep_ids  <- unique(loc_geom$hex_id)

  panel_full <- tidyr::expand_grid(
    hex_id    = keep_ids,
    month_num = months_lv
  ) %>%
    left_join(st_drop_geometry(pm) %>% select(hex_id, month_num, tap_on),
              by = c("hex_id","month_num")) %>%
    mutate(tap_on = coalesce(tap_on, 0)) %>%
    group_by(hex_id) %>%
    mutate(tap_on_s = if (stats::sd(tap_on) > 0) as.numeric(scale(tap_on)) else tap_on) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    mutate(tap_on_s_jit = tap_on_s + rnorm(n(), sd = jitter_sd))

  # 4) Build a space–time cube
  cube <- sfdep::spacetime(
    panel_full,
    loc_geom %>% select(hex_id),
    .loc_col  = "hex_id",
    .time_col = "month_num"
  )
  stopifnot(sfdep::is_spacetime_cube(cube))

  # 5) Neighbors/weights: use KNN to guarantee connectivity (no isolates)
  pts <- tryCatch(st_point_on_surface(loc_geom), error = function(e) st_centroid(loc_geom))
  n   <- nrow(pts)
  best_nb <- NULL; best_k <- NA_integer_; best_comp <- NA_integer_; best_zero <- NA

  for (k_try in 8:20) {
    nb_try   <- sfdep::st_knn(pts, k = min(k_try, max(1, n-1)))
    zero_deg <- any(spdep::card(nb_try) == 0)
    comps    <- spdep::n.comp.nb(nb_try)$nc
    if (!zero_deg && comps == 1) { best_nb <- nb_try; best_k <- k_try; best_comp <- comps; best_zero <- zero_deg; break }
  }
  if (is.null(best_nb)) {
    best_k   <- min(20, max(1, n-1))
    best_nb  <- sfdep::st_knn(pts, k = best_k)
    best_comp <- spdep::n.comp.nb(best_nb)$nc
    best_zero <- any(spdep::card(best_nb) == 0)
  }
  wt <- sfdep::st_weights(best_nb, style = "W")

  cube_nb <- cube %>%
    sfdep::activate("geometry") %>%
    mutate(nb = best_nb, wt = wt, .before = 1) %>%
    sfdep::set_nbs("nb") %>%
    sfdep::set_wts("wt")

  message(sprintf("[EHSA %s] KNN k=%d | comp=%d | zero-degree=%s | T=%d",
                  target_slot, best_k, best_comp, best_zero, length(months_lv)))

  # 6) Run EHSA on the standardized + jittered variable
  ehsa_out <- suppressWarnings(
    sfdep::emerging_hotspot_analysis(
      x    = cube_nb,
      .var = "tap_on_s_jit",
      k    = k_lag,
      nsim = nsim
    )
  )

  # 7) Join EHSA result back to geometry and tag the slot label
  res_sf <- loc_geom %>%
    left_join(ehsa_out, by = c("hex_id" = "location")) %>%
    mutate(slot = target_slot)

  # 8) Quick summary: count significant cells (p < 0.05)
  n_sig <- res_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(!is.na(p_value) & p_value < 0.05) %>% nrow()
  message(sprintf("[EHSA %s] significant (p<0.05): %d / %d", target_slot, n_sig, nrow(res_sf)))

  return(res_sf)
}

# Batch-run EHSA for the three time slots
slots_lv <- c("WKDY_AM_06_09","WKDY_PM_17_20","WKND_11_20")
ehsa_all <- map_dfr(slots_lv, run_ehsa_for_slot)

# Plot helper: show each slot (highlighting only significant cells)
plot_ehsa_slot <- function(ehsa_sf, target_slot, title_prefix = "Emerging Hot Spots") {
  ehsa_one <- ehsa_sf %>% filter(slot == target_slot)
  ehsa_sig <- ehsa_one %>% filter(!is.na(p_value) & p_value < 0.05)

  if (nrow(ehsa_sig) == 0) {
    tm_shape(ehsa_one) +
      tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", border.col = "white") +
      tm_title(paste0(title_prefix, " — ", target_slot, " (no p<0.05 cells)")) +
      tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
  } else {
    tm_shape(ehsa_one) +
      tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", border.col = "white") +
    tm_shape(ehsa_sig) +
      tm_polygons(fill = "classification") +
      tm_title(paste0(title_prefix, " — ", target_slot)) +
      tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
  }
}

# Render maps for AM, PM, and Weekend
map_am <- plot_ehsa_slot(ehsa_all, "WKDY_AM_06_09",  "Emerging Hot Spots (2025-07…09)")
map_pm <- plot_ehsa_slot(ehsa_all, "WKDY_PM_17_20",  "Emerging Hot Spots (2025-07…09)")
map_wk <- plot_ehsa_slot(ehsa_all, "WKND_11_20",     "Emerging Hot Spots (2025-07…09)")

# Print to viewer (tmap: print each map explicitly)
print(map_am); print(map_pm); print(map_wk)
# Summary: Check EHSA classification results
ehsa_summary <- ehsa_all %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(p_value) & p_value < 0.05) %>%
  count(slot, classification) %>%
  arrange(slot, desc(n))

knitr::kable(ehsa_summary, caption = "Significant EHSA Classifications by Time Slot (p < 0.05)")
Significant EHSA Classifications by Time Slot (p < 0.05)
slot classification n

The Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) was performed to examine temporal changes in bus passenger demand across three periods: weekday morning (6–9 AM), weekday evening (5–8 PM), and weekend/holiday (11 AM–8 PM). Local Gi* statistics were first computed at the 375 m hexagon level to detect spatial clusters of high and low trip volumes. These Gi* values were then evaluated using the Mann–Kendall test to identify intensifying or diminishing hotspot trends over time.

The analysis found no statistically significant (p < 0.05) temporal trends across all three time periods, indicating that bus travel patterns remained stable from July to September 2025. Most hexagons were classified as “No Pattern” or “Sporadic,” showing minimal spatial change in passenger concentration. High-demand zones such as the CBD, Tampines, and Jurong East continued to dominate, while peripheral regions maintained low activity.

Overall, the EHSA results suggest a mature and steady urban mobility structure, where commuting flows are well-established and consistent. This implies that existing transport services are effectively meeting current demand, and that future adjustments should focus on minor operational refinements rather than major route changes.

5. Conclusion

This study analyzed Singapore’s bus boarding patterns from July to September 2025 using a 375m hexagonal grid, aiming to uncover fine-grained spatial and temporal trends in passenger activity. By systematically applying both Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), the study identified localized clustering and temporal change patterns that could not be captured through global statistics alone.

The LMSA results revealed statistically significant (p < 0.05) high-demand hot spots (High-High) in the Central Business District (CBD), Tampines, Jurong East, and Woodlands during the weekday morning peak (6–9 a.m.), while low-demand cold spots (Low-Low) were observed in industrial zones such as Tuas and Jurong Island. The Getis–Ord Gi* statistic further quantified the strength and persistence of these clusters, indicating distinct directional flows — north-to-south commuting toward the CBD in the morning, reverse movements during the evening peak, and leisure-oriented mobility toward Orchard, Tampines, and other retail centers on weekends.

Although EHSA was applied across a short three-month window, no statistically significant (p < 0.05) temporal trends were detected. The spatial configuration of hot and cold spots remained stable, suggesting short-term stability rather than long-term persistence. A longer time horizon (e.g., 12 months) is recommended to identify emerging or diminishing trends with stronger statistical power.

Based on these findings, several operational and planning insights can be drawn:

  • Morning peak: Increase feeder bus frequency and expand transfer-hub capacity in northern neighborhoods.

  • Weekend periods: Introduce shuttle services connecting suburban areas to regional shopping centers.

  • Long-term strategy: Monitor demand growth in former cold-spot regions and prioritize proactive infrastructure investment.

In conclusion, the integrated use of LMSA and EHSA provides a robust data-driven framework for precise demand forecasting and adaptive public transport service design in Singapore. Future studies could extend the analysis to a longer time frame and incorporate additional datasets, such as alighting and smart-card records, to capture the full journey dynamics of urban mobility.
